newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: LME zinc seen testing $1,600 - Asian trade.
newsitem.headline: LME zinc seen testing $1,600 - Asian trade.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) zinc prices are expected to move higher later on Thursday to test resistance at $1,600 a tonne, supported by the prevailing squeeze in September dates onwards, Asian dealers said.
"We believe three-month LME zinc will test resistance at $1,600 and then will see a correction on the current upward trend," a dealer with Tong Yang Futures said.
He said zinc's cash-to-three months backwardation flared up to $20/$25 in Wednesday afternoon's LME ring before pulling back to $17, which would give the metal good support to clear a path to $1,600.

Another Seoul trader said large zinc shorts, widely believed to be held by Chinese smelters, were expected to prompt more borrowing and to widen the current backwardation as the prompt month for the shorts was believed to be from September onwards.
The trader said the borrowing and short-covering, along with good consumer demand, would boost zinc despite the market being very overbought on the charts.

The 14-day relative strength index (RSI) for three-month zinc stood at 81.58 percent on Wednesday from 80.66 percent the previous day. The market generally considers an RSI of 70 or more as overbought and 30 or less as oversold.
Zinc prices rose to $1,552/$1,557 at 0600 GMT from the previous day's late LME close of $1,550/$1,555.

LME Broker Rudolf Wolff said in its daily report that zinc hit a new seven-year high of $1,556 on Wednesday, which, coupled with the positive close and the technical indicators maintaining their upward bias, suggested further upward challenges.
LME broker Macquarie said: "The zinc industry is now more profitable than the copper industry."

According to analysts Brook Hunt, the average break-even cost for the Western copper industry is around $1,764 a tonne, implying an average margin of 34 percent based on Wednesday's price. For zinc, break-even was pegged at $1,060 a tonne, implying an average margin of 49 percent, Macquarie said.
Traders said nickel prices were unlikely to be affected by reports that talks between Canada's Falconbridge Ltd and the union for its workers had broken off contract talks.

A Canadian newspaper reported contract talks between Falconbridge Ltd and the union representing more than 1,400 at the nickel miner's Sudbury workers broke down on Wednesday after the union angrily left the bargaining table.
Earlier on Wednesday Falconbridge director of human resources Gerald Foley told Reuters talks were still on track and a deal could be reached before the August 1 strike deadline.
Falconbridge's Sudbury operations produced 42,100 tonnes of nickel, 48,800 tonnes of copper and 730 tonnes of cobalt last year.

"We do not expect that the reports will affect the nickel market as physical demand for nickel has not been good," said a trader with South Korea's largest steel maker Pohang Iron and Steel Co Ltd (POSCO).
"We expect the talks to begin soon and to be settled in the near future as they were in Inco's case," he added.
But the POSCO trader said the reports could give some support to nickel prices.
Meanwhile, three-month aluminium prices were expected to stay in a range between $1,550 and $1,650, traders said.
Three-month aluminium bid prices were flat at $1,641 at 0600 GMT in Asian trade from Wednesday's late LME close.
LME broker Brandeis said resistance was seen at $1,650. If this level is breached on Thursday, the next target on the upside is $1,675.
Copper prices were expected to stay flat as the cash to threes backwardation has eased from last week's peak of $270 to $60/$65 on Wednesday, traders said.
"The copper backwardation has been eased due to lending as the market is in the low seasonal demand summer perio," a trader with a major trading house said.
Three-month copper prices edged up to $2,274 a tonne on Thursday in Asian trade from late Wednesday's lower close of $2,273.
"We expect copper stocks will not increase further as the current backwardation appears unattractive," the trader said.
-- Jae Hur, Seoul Newsroom (822) 727 5651
